passages.t: ‘God is our refuge and strength’, though the mountains fall
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. Of the sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. A song” (verse 1). Then the psalm states its whole faith in one line. “God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble” (verse 1).

From that comes a bold ‘therefore’. “Therefore we will not fear, though the earth is transformed and the mountains are toppled into the depths of the seas” (verse 2). The waters “roar and foam and the mountains quake in the surge” (verse 3).

Then a pause: Selah.

The worst thing a person could picture is set out here. The ground itself gives way. The psalm does not say this will never happen. It says that even then, God is a refuge.
passages.hearers:
‘Alamoth’ is a word for music. It also appears where some players “were to play the harps according to Alamoth” (1 Chronicles 15:20). It looks like the Hebrew for ‘young women’, so many think it meant a high range of voice or instrument. No one is sure. The book page explains these musical words.

To the first hearers, mountains were the most solid things in the world. The sea stood for chaos and danger. So mountains falling into the sea is the world coming apart. The psalm uses the biggest picture it can find.

The word ‘refuge’ means a place to run and hide. ‘Strength’ is power to stand. ‘An ever-present help’ is, more exactly, ‘a help that is very much found’ in trouble. God is not far away when trouble comes. He is there to be found.
passages.later:
When Jesus stilled a storm, the sea was the danger. “Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the sea. ‘Silence!’ He commanded. ‘Be still!’ And the wind died down” (Mark 4:39).

The last pages of the Bible picture a world where chaos is gone: “the sea was no more” (Revelation 21:1).
passages.asks:
The psalm does not tell you not to fear because nothing bad will happen. It tells you not to fear because of who is with you when it does.

What would ‘the mountains toppling’ be for you? A diagnosis, a loss, a family coming apart? Say verse 1 into that. It is not a way to make the trouble small. It is a way to put God next to it.

passages.t: ‘There is a river’, and ‘The LORD of Hosts is with us’
passages.happening:
The picture changes from a raging sea to a gentle river. “There is a river whose streams delight the city of God, the holy place where the Most High dwells” (verse 4).

“God is within her; she will not be moved. God will help her when morning dawns” (verse 5). Around the city, things fall apart. “Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts when He lifts His voice” (verse 6).

Then comes the refrain. “The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Here is something a first hearer would know. Jerusalem has no river. Its water came from a spring and from rain stored in cisterns. So the ‘river’ is a picture. It recalls the river that watered Eden: “Now a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden” (Genesis 2:10). The prophet Ezekiel later saw water flowing from the temple (Ezekiel 47:1). Where God lives, life flows.

‘The LORD of Hosts’ names God as the commander of armies, in heaven and on earth. ‘With us’ in Hebrew is immanu. It is the first part of the name Immanuel, ‘God with us’, in Isaiah 7:14.

No event is named. Many have linked the psalm to the time Assyria surrounded Jerusalem and the city was spared (2 Kings 18 and 19). Others think it was simply sung at the temple. The psalm does not say.
passages.later:
Matthew tells of the birth of Jesus and quotes Isaiah: “they will call Him Immanuel” (Matthew 1:23). Matthew explains that the name means ‘God with us’. The same Gospel ends with Jesus' promise, “And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

The river comes back at the end of the Bible: “a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1).
passages.hard: Does this psalm promise that any city or country will never fall? No. ‘The city of God’ here is the place where God chose to dwell among his people, not a promise about any modern place or nation. Jerusalem itself was later destroyed by Babylon, and the prophets said plainly why. The psalm's confidence rests on God being present, not on walls. The book page notes that no reading of these psalms gives any modern nation God's place.
passages.asks:
The river is quiet. It does not roar like the sea. God's help often comes like that: steady and small, morning by morning, while the nations make all the noise.

The refrain is in the plural: ‘with us’. This psalm is for a people together, not only one person alone. Who do you need to stand with you, and say it with you?

passages.t: ‘Be still, and know that I am God’
passages.happening:
Now the people are invited to look. “Come, see the works of the LORD, who brings devastation upon the earth” (verse 8). The devastation turns out to be the end of war. “He makes wars to cease throughout the earth; He breaks the bow and shatters the spear; He burns the shields in the fire” (verse 9).

Then God himself speaks. “Be still and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth” (verse 10).

The refrain comes once more. “The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Bows, spears and shields were the weapons of every ancient army. God does not just win a battle here. He destroys the weapons of the whole earth.

‘Be still’ is a well-loved line, and it is often read as a call to quiet prayer. The Hebrew word, harpu, is stronger and plainer than that. It means ‘let go’, ‘stop’, or ‘drop your hands’. Some Bibles put it as ‘cease striving’. In this psalm it is spoken in the middle of war. It is first a command to the warring nations: stop fighting, and know who is God. It is also a word to God's own people, who are tempted to fear or to fight in their own strength.

Martin Luther's hymn known in English as ‘A Mighty Fortress Is Our God’ was drawn from this psalm.
passages.later:
Moses told Israel at the Red Sea, “The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still” (Exodus 14:14).

Isaiah looked to a day when the nations “will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks” (Isaiah 2:4). Psalm 46 sings of the same hope: wars ended by God himself.
passages.asks:
‘Be still’ is not first about feeling calm. It is about letting go of control: the plans, the worry, the fight you think you must win alone. Stop, and know who is God.

Quiet prayer is a good way to do that. But the psalm also asks something harder. What are you gripping that God is asking you to drop?
